instructions: Score each item with quality-rubric.md. input, when present, is the problem the item's tree answers; chain lists the reasons above it, from the top; siblings are the other reasons answering the same why.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: Alerting fires only on errors the job emits, so a run that never starts sends no signal and no expected-heartbeat check exists.
After noisy backup pages, the team deliberately narrowed alert rules to hard errors, and a heartbeat check was seen as reintroducing noise.
items.reason: A heartbeat would need maintenance-window silences, and nobody wanted to keep a suppression calendar for the database host current.
siblings: Planned maintenance windows repeatedly paged on-call for expected backup interruptions, prompting the rules to be trimmed to fatal errors only.
On-call health is measured by page count, so any check that could add pages lacked a sponsor willing to propose it.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: No one owns scheduled restore drills, so backup files are never opened or counted until an actual outage forces a restore.
items.reason: The backup cron was set up by one engineer, and ownership never passed to a team when that engineer moved on.
siblings: Restore drills appear in no team's sprint goals or on-call runbook, so they lose every scheduling contest against feature work.
No environment exists that can hold a full restore, so each drill would first need infrastructure nobody has budgeted.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: The wrapper script exits 0 on a stale lock file or missed cron window, so skipped runs look like successes.
The author coded the lock-held and outside-window branches as deliberate exit 0 no-ops to stop cron from mailing on expected overlaps.
items.reason: The wrapper was reviewed as a small shell utility, so no reviewer questioned what each guard branch's exit status told the scheduler.
siblings: Early versions exited non-zero when a long dump overran the next slot, flooding the ops inbox with cron mail until someone silenced it.
The start-window guard was added quickly to keep dumps off daytime production load and copied the lock branch's existing exit 0.

items.input: Our nightly database backup job silently skips some runs, and nobody notices until a restore is needed.
items.question: why
chain: Alerting fires only on errors the job emits, so a run that never starts sends no signal and no expected-heartbeat check exists.
The schedule lives only in one host's crontab, so monitoring holds no record of which nightly runs are expected.
items.reason: No inventory of scheduled jobs exists, so reviews of monitoring coverage never list the backup job as needing a heartbeat.
siblings: The job predates the team's adoption of a scheduler with run history, and migrating legacy cron jobs was deprioritized as already working.
The database team owns the crontab while the platform team owns alerting, and neither backlog includes wiring expected-run checks between them.

items.question: why
chain: The wrapper script exits 0 on a stale lock file or missed cron window, so skipped runs look like successes.
items.reason: The lock is a bare file with no PID or age check, so a crashed run's leftover lock looks identical to a live run.
siblings: The author coded the lock-held and outside-window branches as deliberate exit 0 no-ops to stop cron from mailing on expected overlaps.
The wrapper's exit contract has only success and failure, with no distinct skipped status that cron or a dashboard could recognise.
